notes.read: A misty autumn birch grove: the mood is the soft blue-gray fog with a low sun glowing at the upper left, and the subject is the leaf-covered path going back into it between pale birches. The hard parts are keeping the far things soft and cool, the floor full of leaves without painting each one, and the big birches crisp and white without outlining them. The lesson should be about painting back to front: haze, far wood, floor, then the trunks and gold leaves on top.
notes.order: Back to front, as the paint-along technique works: the whole canvas is blended as fog first, then the far dark wood and its misty edge, the floor and path, the faint far birches, the bushes and the boulder, the leaf carpet, the five big birches over a finished ground, and last the hanging leaves and palest lights, which sit in front of everything.

steps.blend-mist: The fog sits behind everything, so it covers the canvas first, wet, in one blend.
steps.dab-dark-wood: The far tree line is the next thing back; its dark mass goes on dry mist so it stays soft.
steps.mist-wood-edge: Right after the dark wood, a lighter rim melts it into the fog so it reads as far away.
steps.lay-floor: The ground has to be down before the path, bushes, rock and leaves go on it.
steps.lay-path: The path is laid on the dry floor so it keeps its edge and narrows into the fog.
steps.pull-far-birches: The thin far trunks stand in the fog behind the bushes, so they go before the undergrowth.
steps.mark-far-birches: Their soft bark marks follow while the brush and stroke are the same.
steps.dab-dark-undergrowth: The bushes cover the far trunks' feet, so they come after them; dark dabs first.
steps.dab-gold-undergrowth: The gold clusters sit on the dry dark dabs as the lit leaves.
steps.build-rock: The boulder sits in front of the olive band, so it comes after the undergrowth, as one flat shape.
steps.moss-rock: The moss goes on the dry boulder, the light on its top.
steps.dash-rust-leaves: The leaf carpet is built darkest first, over the finished floor, path and rock foot.
steps.dash-ochre-leaves: The lighter leaves go over the dry rust ones so both show.
steps.pull-big-birches: The focal trunks go on over a finished ground so they stay the sharpest things in the picture.
steps.shade-big-birches: Shade goes on the dry pale trunks before the bark marks.
steps.mark-big-bark: The dark bark marks go over the shade, heaviest at the feet.
steps.light-big-bark: The light rim comes last on the trunks, over the marks in places.
steps.dab-hanging-leaves: The hanging leaves cross over the trunks, so they come after them.
steps.tip-pale-leaves: The palest taps sit on the dry gold leaves as the last lights at the top.
steps.dash-pale-leaves: The brightest floor leaves go on last, over everything on the ground; the painting is finished.

stages.name: Blend the misty glow
steps: Start in the upper left corner of the canvas with Pale gold, working a small patch of soft glow there.
Work in short criss-cross X strokes, then move out across the canvas. Pick up Haze blue and Deep haze blue without rinsing, so each colour melts into the last while wet.
Keep Pale gold to a faint warmth near the left edge, where the hazy sun sits. Haze blue fills the middle; Deep haze blue goes into the lower part and the right side of the canvas.
Leave no white canvas anywhere: cover every corner. Let a few paler upright streaks show through the blue, like trunks far back in the fog.
Stop when the whole canvas is a soft blue-gray mist with gentle criss-cross texture and no hard edges.

Leave the fog and the dark wood untouched. Keep the line where the floor meets the fog level and soft, not a hard stripe.
Stop when the lower part of the canvas is a warm, slightly mottled floor about 4 3/4 in tall, with no path or leaf marks yet.

opening.welcome: You're about to paint a misty autumn birch grove, with a leafy path running back into the fog. What makes it sing is the contrast: two big leaning white birches, crisp and sharp, standing in front of a soft, glowing haze.
opening.light: A hazy low sun glows through the mist from behind the trees. It lights one side of each trunk, each bush and each leaf cluster, and leaves the other side in soft gray shade.

skills.how: Press the full width of the brush, then turn onto its edge and ease off, so the mark starts wide and tapers. It makes every birch trunk, far and near, and every bark mark. Keep the pressure changing through the stroke, or the line comes out the same width all the way.

Only the tip of a dry brush goes in the paint, and you skim lightly so the mark breaks up on the canvas texture. It builds the far wood, its misty rim, and the shade and light on the big trunks. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and skim the base color back over it.

Keep the brush level and the strokes going side to side, so the ground lies flat and stretches away. It lays the path and every fallen leaf in the carpet. Keep the strokes shorter and calmer toward the fog, and bigger and busier nearest you.

opening.road: First the fog goes on as one wet blend over the whole canvas, so the mood is down before anything else. Then the far wood, the forest floor, the path and the faint far birches go in, all soft and cool because they sit back in the mist. Next come the golden bushes and the mossy boulder, then the carpet of fallen leaves. The big birches go on near the end, over a finished ground, so they stay the sharpest and brightest things in the picture. Last, the hanging gold leaves and the palest lights go in front of everything.

the-misty-distance.for: This stage sets the mood: the soft fog and the dark far wood that everything else will sit in front of.
the-misty-distance.end: The canvas is a soft blue-gray fog with faint ghost trunks, and a dark blue-green wood melting into the mist at its rim.

the-forest-floor.for: This stage gives the scene its ground: a warm floor and the path that leads your eye back into the fog.
the-forest-floor.end: A warm orange floor now meets the fog, with a plain mauve path narrowing back into the mist.

the-far-birches.for: This stage adds depth with thin, pale birches far back in the fog, kept soft so they stay distant.
the-far-birches.end: Three thin pale birches stand in the fog by the path, dark at their feet and lightly speckled higher up.

the-golden-undergrowth.for: This stage brings in the autumn color: banks of golden bushes and a mossy boulder by the path.
the-golden-undergrowth.end: A bank of golden bushes glows by the path, an olive band sits at the foot of the dark wood, and a mossy boulder rests in front of it.

the-leaf-carpet.for: This stage turns the plain floor into a carpet of fallen leaves that draws you down the path.
the-leaf-carpet.end: The floor and path are covered in rust and ochre leaves, big and busy in front and calmer toward the fog.

the-big-birches.for: This stage paints the star of the picture: the big white birches, sharp and bright in front of the soft scene.
the-big-birches.end: Five big birches stand in front, pale and shaded, with dark broken bark marks and a warm rim of light.

the-last-lights.for: This stage finishes the painting with the hanging gold leaves and the last, brightest touches of light.
the-last-lights.end: Gold leaves hang across the trees, bright gold fills the bushes, and pale sunlit leaves dot the floor: the painting is finished.

technique_picks.technique_why: A misty wood is a classic paint-along: a wet blended haze first, then soft far shapes, then the pale birches and gold leaves built up in dabs and dashes over it, all with a few brushes and repeated marks a beginner can make.
